root_cause.text: In the `wave5_vpu_remove` function, video device unregistration was performed after disabling PM runtime and powering down hardware, allowing the worker thread (triggered by hrtimer in polling mode) to read hardware registers on a powered-down device, causing a synchronous external abort and kernel panic.
root_cause.evidence: The patch moves `wave5_vpu_enc_unregister_device`, `wave5_vpu_dec_unregister_device`, and `v4l2_device_unregister` to the beginning of `wave5_vpu_remove`, before the PM runtime disable, clock disabling, and reset assertion. The commit message explicitly states: "The original cleanup order disabled PM runtime and powered down hardware before unregistering video devices. When autosuspend triggers and powers off the hardware, the video devices are still registered and the worker thread can still be triggered by the hrtimer, causing it to attempt reading registers from powered-off hardware." This matches the crash trace showing `wave5_vdi_read_register` being called from `wave5_vpu_irq_work_fn`.

candidates.rationale: Power down hardware before unregistering video devices, allowing a concurrently running worker thread to access powered-down registers and cause a synchronous abort.
Disables clocks and powers down the hardware before video device unregistration, so any ongoing hardware access (e.g., from a worker thread) triggers an abort.
Performs video device unregistration after hardware has been powered down, violating the required order and allowing a worker thread to read registers on a powered-down device.
Same as encoder unregistration – called after power-down, so any residual worker thread activity accesses powered-down hardware.
Unregisters the V4L2 device after hardware power-down; may allow the worker thread to trigger register reads on the powered-down device.
Releases the video device interface after power-down, potentially exposing the device to worker thread register access.

vuln_statements.explanation: This statement powers down the hardware (asserts reset) before unregistering video devices, creating a window where a concurrently running worker thread may access hardware registers on a powered-down device and cause a synchronous external abort.

This statement disables and unprepares clocks, effectively powering down the hardware before video device unregistration, leaving the hardware inaccessible while worker threads may still attempt register reads.

This statement unregisters the encoder video device after hardware power-down, violating the required order. Any worker thread activity that reads hardware registers after this point will access a powered-down device, leading to a crash.

This statement unregisters the decoder video device after hardware power-down. Similar to encoder, it allows residual worker thread register reads on powered-down hardware, causing a synchronous abort.

This statement unregisters the V4L2 device after hardware power-down, potentially allowing worker thread accesses to hardware registers on the powered-down device via the unregistered but still active V4L2 device.

This statement releases the video device interface after hardware power-down, after all previous cleanup steps. Any lingering worker thread that triggers hardware register reads at this point will still access powered-down hardware and cause a panic.
